feedback.body: Thabo, you calculated the expression strictly from left to right, which led to the wrong answer. Remember that multiplication and division should be done before addition and subtraction, regardless of their position. Try working through the problem again, focusing on completing all multiplication and division steps first before moving on to addition and subtraction. This will help you get the correct result.

You tried to add fractions by adding the top numbers and the bottom numbers separately, but this is not how fractions are combined. When adding fractions, the pieces must be the same size before you can count them together. Try cutting paper strips into equal pieces to see how fractions add up. Also, remember that when something is doubled, all parts must be doubled, not just added on.

You treated negative numbers as if they were positive when ordering them, which changed your answers. Try drawing a number line and remember that numbers further to the left are smaller. You also moved the decimal point the wrong number of places when adding decimals. Next, count the zeros in the number you multiply by to know how many places to move the decimal point.

You are reading the percentage sign as a decimal point, which changes the value. Remember that percent means out of one hundred, so you should divide by one hundred first when converting percentages. Also, when adding fractions, you added the top numbers and the bottom numbers separately, which is not correct. Try cutting paper strips into equal pieces to see how fractions can be added only when the pieces are the same size.

Chen, in your work, you subtracted numbers when simplifying fractions instead of dividing them. Remember, simplifying means dividing both the top and bottom by the same number to split into equal groups. Also, when comparing decimals, you treated the digits after the decimal point as whole numbers. Try writing both decimals with the same number of digits after the decimal point and then compare them column by column.

Kwame, you made a few mistakes in your math work. You ignored the brackets, which means you didn't calculate what's inside them before moving on. Try working out the value inside the brackets first and write that down before doing anything else. Also, when you add fractions, remember that you cannot just add the tops and bottoms separately; try cutting paper strips into equal pieces to see how to add fractions properly.

You made a small mistake when converting to a percentage by calculating the final multiplication incorrectly. The way you approached the problem is correct, so please try recalculating just the last multiplication step. Also, when adding fractions, you combined the numerators and denominators directly, which is not how fractions work. To understand this better, try cutting two paper strips into different numbers of equal parts and practice adding those pieces only when they are the same size.

You dropped the brackets when rewriting the expression, which made it hard to follow your working. Also, you treated subtracting a negative number incorrectly, and you divided by the wrong number when sharing the total. To improve, try writing the brackets down carefully in every step until you simplify what's inside. This will help keep your work clear and accurate.

You wrote 6/8 where a mixed number was needed, but the value is correct. Next time, try to show how many whole groups you can take out from the numerator to write it as a whole number and a leftover fraction. Also, remember that when adding fractions, you cannot just add the top and bottom numbers separately. Try cutting paper strips into equal pieces to see how only pieces of the same size can be added together. Finally, when working with ratios, think about multiplying all parts of the recipe instead of just adding extra amounts.

Also, when you find a common denominator for fractions, remember to multiply the numerators by the same number you multiply the denominators by, so the fractions stay equivalent. Next time, focus on keeping the brackets in place and scaling both parts of the fraction properly when finding a common denominator.
